title: The Encyclopedie
text:
In 1747 a group of Paris publishers, who had planned simply to translate an English reference work, gave the job of editing it to two men: the writer Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert. They turned it into something far more ambitious, a complete survey of human knowledge, the sciences, the trades and the arts, written in a spirit of reason and open inquiry.

The first volume appeared in 1751. Contributors included Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and many specialists, physicians and craftsmen, some of them anonymous. Diderot visited workshops to learn how trades actually worked, and the volumes of engraved plates showed tools and processes in precise detail.

The work soon ran into trouble. In 1752 the royal government suspended it. In 1759 its privilege to publish was revoked and the Pope condemned it. D'Alembert withdrew, exhausted by the attacks. Diderot carried on almost alone, with the tireless help of the Chevalier Louis de Jaucourt, who wrote thousands of articles himself. The director of the book trade, Malesherbes, is said to have warned Diderot of a raid and hidden the manuscripts in his own house. Diderot later discovered that his own publisher had secretly cut passages from proofs to avoid trouble, and he was furious.

The remaining text volumes were printed quietly and released together in 1765, and the last plates came out in 1772. The finished work ran to seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates.
lesson: A long collective project survives setbacks when a core of committed people keeps going. One or two persistent members can carry a team through years of opposition.
people: Denis Diderot, Jean le Rond d'Alembert, Louis de Jaucourt, Malesherbes
source: Encyclopedie, ou dictionnaire raisonne des sciences, des arts et des metiers (1751 to 1772); Philipp Blom, Enlightening the World (2004)
